newsitem.title: USA: US House members lay ground for electricity debate.
newsitem.headline: US House members lay ground for electricity debate.

text.p: Amid the flurry to close the 104th Congress, two House members introduced bills to open the electricity market to competition, weighing in on an issue set to dominate the Commerce Committee's agenda next year.

Republican Rep. Tom DeLay of Texas and Democratic Rep. Frank Pallone of New Jersey added their own twists to a list of proposals for breaking electric utility monopolies and repealing laws governing utility holdings and power production.
"Everybody's throwing markers out there for next year," said Buddy Eller, a spokesman for Southern Co.
House Commerce Committee chairman Thomas Bliley, a Virginia Republican, this week reiterated that opening retail power markets to competition would be a top priority next year.
As House Republican Whip, DeLay staked out a position for the House Republican leadership.

"A member of House leadership has recognized the issue has to be dealt with in the 105th Congress," said Dana Perino, spokeswoman for Republican Rep. Dan Schaefer, who introduced the House's first sweeping electricity industry reform bill.
"It's very encouraging for us," she said.
In contrast to Schaefer's bill which called for all consumers to be able to choose their power suppliers by the end of 2000, DeLay's bill called for consumer choice by January 1, 1998.

DeLay also proposed barring utilities from recouping stranded costs -- investments which might become uneconomic in the new market -- while Schaefer called for letting state regulators decide how to handle the multibillion dollar issue.
Schaefer, chairman of the energy and power panel which would lead off the electricity debate, had no comment on the bill by Rep. Pallone, the top Democrat on the House panel.

Pallone's bill laid out his and other Northeastern lawmakers' concerns about the environmental impact of encouraging cheap power production from dirty coal plants in the Midwest, which could worsen pollution in the Northeast.
The bill calls for changing the Clean Air Act before moving to open the retail power market to competition.

"If you're changing the regulatory regime for electricity that underlay the last Clean Air Act, then you have to change the Clean Air Act," said Rick Kessler, a senior aide to Pallone, referring to utility emission standards in the law.
"If you want to sell outside your service territory and outside your state, then you've got to deal with pollution outside your territory and outside your state," he said.
